title: The new economics of enterprise AI
summary: Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from “can we use it?” to “h…
body: Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from “can we use it?” to “how efficiently are we using it?” Enterprise AI is going through the same shift. What began as isolated chatbot and copilot experiments is becoming a foundational layer of the business, with models, agents, and data increasingly interconnected in production workloads. The important question stops being what a token or GPU-hour costs. It becomes how efficiently the AI environment converts paid capacity into useful business outcomes. That’s the metric worth tracking: effective cost per useful outcome — the total platform, model, operations, and capacity cost required to complete work the business can actually use, whether a resolved request or a completed workflow. Three ways to run AI Utilization is central to the economics. title: Ultrasound waves that jiggle deep brain structures may relieve delusions in schizophrenia, small trial hints
summary: In a new pilot study, 10 minutes of transcranial ultrasound stimulation reduced patients' delusion severity, scientists report.
body: Stimulating the brain with ultrasound could help counter the delusions people experience in schizophrenia, a small trial finds. The trial involved transcranial ultrasound stimulation, in which a device placed on a patient's head delivers ultrasound waves through the skull and into the brain. Its goal is to change the activity in a targeted brain region. Delusions are false beliefs that are very difficult to shake; for example, a person might believe they are being stalked when they aren't or think that a major disaster is about to occur without any evidence to suggest so. In the trial, researchers found that a 10-minute session of the ultrasound treatment reduced the severity of delusions for at least a week in patients with schizophrenia or a related disorder. This targeted ultrasound treatment delivered directly to the brain could avoid some of the full-body effects of antipsychotic medications, such as weight gain and high blood pressure . That said, the new results, published Tuesday (Oct. 20) in the journal npj Acoustics , are a first step and will need further verification in larger trials. title: A gene variant triples the risk of getting Alzheimer's disease — fat buildup in brain cells may be to blame, study finds
summary: A gene variant called APOE4 is the biggest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Scientists are finally figuring out how it works.
body: A gene variant called APOE4 dramatically increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer's disease, the most common form of dementia. Now, emerging research is revealing APOE4's true role in the condition, and a new study pinpoints a possible way to treat it. Historically, scientists studying Alzheimer's disease have focused on two proteins that accumulate in patients' brains: amyloid-beta and tau. However, there's a "third thing that people didn't pay attention to, until recently," said study co-author Li-Huei Tsai , a neuroscientist at MIT. That third thing is the accumulation of droplets of fat, or lipids, in the brain, she told Live Science. The APOE gene makes proteins responsible for transporting fat around cells throughout the body and brain. A version of the gene called APOE4, which increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer's three- to 12-fold, makes proteins that are less efficient at this function, Tsai said. But how APOE4 affects different brain cells was not clearly understood. Tsai's team has been working to close that gap for about a decade. "APOE4 can influence many different cell types," she emphasized. "It's not just one cell type." Zeroing in on the clues In past lab…

But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms. title: World's fastest AI-powered racing drone outflies the best human pilots
summary: An AI-operated drone learned to fly from scratch and navigated a race course at speeds over 60 mph, using a single camera.
body: A drone powered by artificial intelligence (AI) has completed a championship race course faster than some of the world's best human drone pilots. In a study published Oct. 14 in the journal Science Robotics , scientists created an AI system capable of pushing a quadcopter through a demanding course at over 60 mph (100 km/h), using little more than a single forward-facing camera, an inertial measurement unit, and a tiny onboard computer. The system, called MonoRace, even won the 2025 Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League drone racing competition, outperforming every rival autonomous team and posting faster times than three former human world-champion drone pilots. MonoRace accomplished this without the aid of GPS, external motion-capture systems, stereo cameras, or a preloaded map of the course. The system is an onboard autonomous flight model created by researchers at the Delft University of Technology's Micro Air Vehicles Lab in the Netherlands. Its name reflects its central design feature; "mono" refers to its monocular vision. title: 'A uniquely direct route that might cause damage': Scientists uncover link between air pollution and eye diseases like glaucoma
summary: A review of 41 studies found that higher exposure to air pollution was linked to greater odds of glaucoma and cataracts, with PM2.5 pollution showing the clearest association.
body: Aging is one of the biggest risk factors for developing glaucoma or cataracts — but as scientists look more closely at what happens to the eyes over a lifetime, they are finding that people's exposure to air pollution also plays a role in whether they develop these eye conditions. Glaucoma, which affects about 80 million people worldwide , is a group of diseases that damage the optic nerve, which carries visual information from the eye to the brain. It can lead to permanent vision loss, usually affecting peripheral vision at first and later central vision. Cataracts are even more common, affecting more than 94 million people globally ; the condition occurs when the eye's lens becomes cloudy, causing blurred vision and, eventually, blindness. Aging raises the risk of both diseases, as do certain medical conditions, such as diabetes. But now, a review of 41 studies suggests that people who are exposed to higher levels of air pollution may also face a greater risk of these diseases. New observations of Pa 30, thought to be the leftovers of a historic supernova called SN 1181, show that its spectacular firework-like filaments are not smooth streams of material. Instead, they consist of chains of tiny gas knots. SN 1181 is so called because astronomers in China and Japan recorded its brief appearance in the year 1181, when they saw it as a naked-eye object in the constellation Cassiopeia. Eight surviving texts date its appearance to between Aug. 4 and 6 of that year. The mysterious object remained visible for 185 days. "It's rare to get this level of detail on a supernova we can date to a specific week in history," Timothy Cunningham , an assistant professor of astronomy and astrophysics at the University of Warwick who led an international team of researchers to study the object, said in a statement . title: Is the brain actually 2 nervous systems smooshed together? A new study claims it is.
summary: A recent study may reshape our understanding of brain evolution and open new avenues for studying neurological diseases.
body: Recent research challenges a long-standing idea about how the brain develops: Rather than arising from a single source, the brain may emerge from two distinct populations of cells, the study finds. "The brain appears as one organ," said study co-author Kyle Loh , an associate professor of developmental biology at Stanford University. "However, we discovered that the front part of the brain and the back part of the brain come from different sources, which are pushed together to create the appearance of a single organ," Loh told Live Science in an email. The findings, published in September in the journal Nature Neuroscience , not only challenge established models of how the brain forms but may also explain why researchers have struggled to grow certain types of brain cells in the laboratory. The scientists say the work could offer new ways to investigate diseases that affect the brainstem, the "stalk" that connects the brain to the spinal cord. summary: Petal, the world's first petabit transoceanic fiber cable, could theoretically support simultaneous music streaming for 75% of the world's population.
body: A new 4,300-mile (7,000-kilometer) undersea fiber cable will shuttle data between the U.S. and France at breakneck speeds of up to 1 million gigabits per second (Gbps) — enough to move around 125 terabytes of data every second, or roughly 25,000 HD movies, each 5 gigabytes large. The cable, called Petal, will be funded and operated by Facebook and Instagram parent company Meta. When it comes online in 2029, the ocean-spanning cable will be the first to deliver petabit capacity — double the capacity of existing subsea cables of this length — across transoceanic distances, Meta representatives said in a statement . That's enough to allow 75% of the world's population to stream music at once. Petal will also be the first commercial subsea cable system to use multi-core fiber technology, according to the statement. Whereas conventional fiber strands typically contain a single core, each of Petal's fiber strands will contain two cores that carry optical signals in opposite directions, allowing a single strand to provide the capacity that would conventionally require a pair of single-core fibers. title: Has there ever been a mountain taller than Everest?
summary: Mount Everest may be the king of the planet today, but has Earth ever thrust a larger mountain from its surface?
body: Sometimes, it takes a great struggle to build towering peaks. And what more thunderous event is there than the clashing of continental plates? Geological pileups have birthed some of the largest and tallest mountains on the planet, including Mount Everest and its Himalayan neighbors. But has there ever been a peak taller than Mount Everest, which stands 29,032 feet (8,849 meters) above sea level? The answer is still a mystery, but there are some geological clues about where the tallest peaks would have been in the ancient past, experts told Live Science. Earth's lost mountains Geologists don't have the level of detail required to pinpoint an exact highest peak hundreds of millions of years ago. "We're never going to get that granularity, unfortunately," Alan Collins , a professor of geology at Adelaide University in Australia, told Live Science. However, clues in residual sediments lodged inside Earth's crust hint at the lost grandeur of primordial snowcaps and summits. Scientists study these crusts to understand how deep they went, which can reveal how tall ancient mountains might have been. summary: Stellar remnants called white dwarfs ‪appear to come in a rainbow of colors, according to a new study.
body: Stellar cores called white dwarfs come in an astonishing array of colors, including what scientists say is the first known green star and the reddest star ever found, new research reveals. A white dwarf star is the dense, cooling core that remains after a low- to medium-mass star runs out of fuel. The new study, published Thursday (Oct. 15) in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments , shows that white dwarfs come in far more colors than their name suggests. White dwarf stars got their moniker because the first known examples glowed in either white or pale blue. The new study, however, suggests that "white" dwarfs also emit visible-light colors like pink, green, cyan, purple and yellow. "Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like 'perfect radiators,' so their colour is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs," Mark Hollands , an astronomer at the University of Warwick in the U.K. and first author of the study, said in a statement . "It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colours nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me." The variety of colors is possible due to whi…

The man, Khaled el-Shahat, immediately notified the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, which sent a team to the village of Behbeit El Hagar to excavate and study the statues, the ministry said in a translated statement . Ramesses II had one of the longest reigns in Egypt's history, ruling from around 1279 to 1213 B.C. During his 66 years in power, Egypt controlled an empire that stretched as far northeast as modern-day Syria. title: Chronic back pain may activate an unexpected brain network, study finds
summary: Movement-induced flares in chronic back pain activate brain regions involved in self-reflection, suggesting chronic pain may be processed differently than acute pain.
body: For people with chronic back pain, everyday movements like bending down to tie their shoes or picking up a grocery bag can trigger painful flare-ups. Now, scientists have made a surprising discovery: These episodes may activate a brain network that's associated with our sense of self. In a new study, the researchers found that movement-induced chronic back pain was tied to increased activity in the brain's default mode network , a group of connected brain regions that lights up during self-reflection and mind wandering. This finding was unexpected because the network typically becomes less active during acute pain, such as transient pain triggered from touching a hot stove or banging your knee on a table. The new study, published Oct. 5 in the British Journal of Anaesthesia , suggests that chronic-pain flare-ups may involve brain processes beyond those responsible for detecting painful sensations. title: Tapeworm drug could help treat endometriosis, mouse study hints
summary: A recent study in mice hints that a modified tapeworm medicine might help relieve painful lesions seen in endometriosis.
body: A modified tapeworm medication could be a promising new treatment for endometriosis, an early study in mice hints. In endometriosis , tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the organ, and these patches of tissue, called "lesions," trigger painful inflammation and heavy menstrual bleeding. In the new study, scientists fitted an anti-worm drug with nanotech armor, and it directly targeted these painful lesions in laboratory mice. The treatment reduced inflammation and slowed or prevented further spread of the lesions, researchers reported in August in the journal Advanced Healthcare Materials . The team is already working on bringing the new drug to clinical trials and hopes this will bring fresh attention to an understudied disease with limited treatment options. Rogue immune cells are a promising drug target Endometriosis is a chronic, hormone-driven condition that affects roughly 10% of reproductive-age females ‪—‬ an estimated 190 million individuals worldwide. title: Hundreds of whale calves have mysteriously died in Patagonia — and scientists are racing to find out why
summary: Scientists are racing to explain why hundreds of southern right whale calves have died this year in Argentine Patagonia, and the first clues are starting to emerge.
body: Since June, more than 300 southern right whale ( Eubalaena australis ) calves have died in Argentine Patagonia, in what scientists describe as an "exceptional" die-off. The preliminary figure already far exceeds the previous annual record set in 2012, when 113 southern right whale calves died — the highest number ever documented for the species , both locally and globally. Now, scientists are racing to figure out exactly what's causing the record-breaking die-off. Laboratory analyses of specimens that died this year tested positive for the pathogenic bacterium Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae , environmental authorities in Chubut province told Live Science. E. rhusiopathiae was first identified in southern right whale calves in 2013 , but scientists don't know what might have changed this year to cause an infection-driven die-off of this magnitude. Researchers say they need to quickly find the answer to better understand the changing threat this species faces, the risk to the wider ecosystem and humans, and what can be done to manage it. title: 'I won't trust AI': Readers share mixed reaction to AI tools that calculate people's biological ages
summary: Scientists have developed AI tools to measure a person's true "biological age." Live Science asked readers whether they would be comfortable using these tools.
body: Scientists are harnessing the power of artificial intelligence (AI) to measure people's biological ages . Unlike chronological age, or the number of years a person has been living, biological age should reflect how well a person's bodily systems are working. Someone with a higher biological age has a higher risk for age-related diseases, such as cancer or dementia , than a person with a younger biological age. While some AI clocks look at epigenetic markers , others focus on other features, like the pitch and pace of people's voices, to calculate a biological age. We recently asked our readers if they would trust such AI tools to measure their biological age. Over 170 people responded, with 44% of voters choosing "Yes, I would take the results with a grain of salt, but it can still provide some helpful insights." The next-largest group, including 23% of voters, also chose a positive answer, clicking the "Yes, I think it would provide useful health information." But readers' comments seemed to reflect the opposite trend, with one commenter writing, "NO!!! Unplug it !!! Heed the warnings!" Another reader posted a similar sentiment, saying: "A.I. is dangerous! The incident has ignited a media firestorm around OpenAI and the launch of an intensifying parliamentary inquiry. title: 1,200-year-old burial in Latvia holds people who died of 'sharp force' injuries, possibly from a Viking raid
summary: A 1,200-year-old burial in Latvia holds the remains of a father, son and four others ‪who may have been victims of a Viking raid.
body: Six people buried in a single grave in Latvia more than 1,000 years ago may have been killed in a bloody Viking raid, a new study suggests. Genetic research into the deceased — four men, a boy and a girl — reveals family connections: The boy was the son of one of the men, while another man was a third-degree relative, perhaps a first cousin or great uncle, the researchers found. The father, the relative, and one other man died from "sharp force" injuries — maybe wounds from an ax or a sword; but it's unknown how the other three individuals died, the researchers reported in the study, which was published in the September issue of the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports . One possibility is that those in the grave were killed in a battle, maybe with a neighboring community. But suspicion also falls on the Vikings: "We will never know if they were killed in a raid, but it remains a possibility because of the date of the grave" and the fatal trauma suffered by three of the men, said study co-author Elīna Pētersone-Gordina , an archaeologist at the University of Latvia.
